rules.reason: The Constitution is the highest authority in the repository. It is amended only through an RFC, a version bump and an ADR — never edited directly.
The ADR log is append-only and immutable (ADR-0000). A decision that proves wrong is superseded by a new ADR, never rewritten. Only new files and supersession metadata should change here.

Tier 0. The invariants E1-E9 and the responsibility matrix are authored here and vendored verbatim by a repository FDOS may not read, so an edit here changes rules on both sides of a boundary only one side can see. Amended only by an RFC here plus an ADR in both repositories (ADR-0023), and every amendment bills the consumer a reviewed re-sync.

An accepted RFC is a historical record like an ADR: it is what a decision was reasoned from, including the arguments that lost and the ones its author withdrew. Editing one rewrites why, which is the part the log exists to keep.

The published contract surface, consumed outside this repository at a pinned version. Any change is a change to somebody else's build, and a breaking one requires an RFC, a consumer issue opened before merge, and an N-1 window (ADR-0024). Not risk-conditional: there is no low-risk edit to a contract others depend on.

The record of what this public repository has revealed about the private side. Editing it changes what is known about a disclosure rather than the disclosure, and a redaction without a record reads as though nothing was ever disclosed.
These are the mechanisms that make the Constitution executable. Weakening a check is indistinguishable from weakening the principle it enforces.
Directory contract front matter is binding, and from M2 it generates the import-boundary configuration. Changing a contract changes what the build permits.

High-risk changes to domain and application code require approval. The published contract surface is covered separately and unconditionally: risk labels are assigned by whoever is making the change, and a contract others build against should not depend on that self-assessment.
High-risk changes to deployment topology require approval.
Secret-like files are blocked by policy. Private institution credentials never share a trust boundary with the public core.
